article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Three principles of the Relationship Centered Schools campaign
description: The Relationship Centered Schools (RCS) campaign, launched in 2015 by Californians for Justice, is a youth-led school transformation initiative organized around three guiding principles. The report states that the campaign "centers three principles to guide action and school improvement: (1) create space for relationship-building, (2) value student voice, and (3) invest in staff." These principles direct how youth organizers, educators, and district leaders collaborate to restructure secondary schools so that students of color and students from low-income backgrounds are known, supported, and able to reach their potential. The campaign has sought to spur transformation in 11 comprehensive high schools across four California regions.
requirements: A community-based organization with youth chapters or after-school programming at school sites to anchor ongoing youth and organizer engagement
constraints: The campaign's approach to change manifests differently in local settings; in Long Beach it operated primarily at the district level while in Fresno it maintained a school-level focus
target_learning_goals: Student motivation and engagement
Sense of belonging and being known by a caring adult
Student agency and voice in school decision-making
examples: Since 2016, CFJ youth organizers have collaborated with district officials, school leaders, and educators in Fresno, Long Beach, Oakland, and San José to advance relationship-centered approaches
key_sources: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856

article_title: Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving
citation: Sifatul Anindho, Videep Venkatesha, Jaclyn Ocumpaugh, and Nathaniel Blanchard. (2026). Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23317
title: Retrospective cued-recall dataset of affective states from 27 participants in 9 groups completing the Weights Task
description: A dataset in which 27 participants in 9 groups of three were video recorded completing the first phase of the Weights Task, a collaborative problem-solving activity adapted from Khebour et al., then individually reviewed their session recording using retrospective cued-recall. Participants reported affective states from a set of seven (Confused, Curious, Frustrated, Disengaged, Optimistic, Surprised, and Conflicted), either voluntarily (self-caught) or after a 60-second inactivity probe (probe-caught), with all reports timestamped. All groups arrived at the correct final solution.
requirements: Video recording of the collaborative session for playback during the recall phase
constraints: The authors state the dataset is relatively small with a proportionately large male population and a fixed set of predefined labels, which may limit generalizability; RCR is susceptible to recall bias and temporal imprecision
target_learners: adult participants over 18 years old, fluent in English, recruited within the authors' department
target_learning_goals: capturing affective dynamics during situated collaborative problem solving
examples: Participants were compensated USD 15 with IRB approval; probe-caught reports constituted 64% and self-caught 36% of reports
key_sources: Sifatul Anindho, Videep Venkatesha, Jaclyn Ocumpaugh, and Nathaniel Blanchard. (2026). Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23317

article_title: Chat or cheat? Academic dishonesty, risk perceptions, and ChatGPT usage in higher education students
citation: Ortiz-Bonnin, S., & Blahopoulou, J. (2025). Chat or cheat? Academic dishonesty, risk perceptions, and ChatGPT usage in higher education students. Social Psychology of Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11218-025-10080-2
title: Rational Choice Theory account of student ChatGPT usage decisions
description: The article applies Rational Choice Theory (Becker, 1968) to explain students' ChatGPT use: "individuals act to maximize personal utility by assessing the potential benefits and costs of different actions." Students weigh benefits such as saving time, reducing effort, or obtaining better grades against costs including likelihood of detection and severity of institutional sanctions. The article pairs RCT with Perceived Academic Dishonesty, arguing RCT captures rational risk-benefit evaluation while PAD captures ethical and normative considerations, and the study's mediation findings are interpreted as consistent with RCT.
requirements: Measures of perceived risk and usage behavior to test the cost-benefit mechanism as operationalized in the study
constraints: The article notes the low detectability of ChatGPT-based plagiarism may weaken the deterrent effect of academic sanctions
Cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation of the modeled relationships
target_learning_goals: ethical decision-making about AI tool use in academic work
examples: The study tested RCT-derived hypotheses H1a/H1b (negative risk-usage links) and H3a/H3b (risk as mediator) in a 468-student survey
key_sources: Ortiz-Bonnin, S., & Blahopoulou, J. (2025). Chat or cheat? Academic dishonesty, risk perceptions, and ChatGPT usage in higher education students. Social Psychology of Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11218-025-10080-2

article_title: How is the Impact of Responsible Conduct of Research Education Evaluated? A Review of Measures Used and a Content Analysis of Outcome Measures with Reported Validation Evidence
citation: M. van Loon, D. Crean, M. van den Hoven, J. Katsarov, N. Evans. (2026). How is the Impact of Responsible Conduct of Research Education Evaluated? A Review of Measures Used and a Content Analysis of Outcome Measures with Reported Validation Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10187-8
title: Framework of reliability and validity evidence categories for classifying RCR outcome-measure validation
description: The review develops a coding framework distinguishing forms of reliability evidence (test–retest, parallel forms, split-half, internal consistency via Cronbach's alpha or Kuder–Richardson formulas) and validity evidence (content validity including cognitive interviews and S-CVIs, face validity, criterion validity, construct validity). It extends the framework of Fenn et al. (2020) with additional categories such as "Global Content Validity Indices (S-CVIs)". The framework was applied so that each measure was coded independently by one reviewer and checked by a second, documenting only explicitly reported evidence.
requirements: Requires retrieving all associated measure materials, including supplementary files, user manuals and earlier development papers, to determine what validation was undertaken
constraints: The protocol focused on documenting only forms of evidence authors explicitly reported; validation was not inferred from statements of intent or general descriptions of test development
target_learning_goals: evaluating the impact of Responsible Conduct of Research education on participants
examples: Applied to classify the 15 identified measures in Table 5, e.g. PDR with Cronbach's alpha 0.84 and parallel-forms correlation 0.70, and REKASA with face and content validity from expert review of 74 draft items
key_sources: M. van Loon, D. Crean, M. van den Hoven, J. Katsarov, N. Evans. (2026). How is the Impact of Responsible Conduct of Research Education Evaluated? A Review of Measures Used and a Content Analysis of Outcome Measures with Reported Validation Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10187-8

article_title: Effective Strategies for Research Integrity Training—a Meta-analysis
citation: Johannes Katsarov, Roberto Andorno, André Krom, Mariëtte van den Hoven. (2021). Effective Strategies for Research Integrity Training—a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:935–955. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09630-9
title: Five-type taxonomy of research-integrity learning outcomes
description: The article organizes RCR training effects into five distinct learning outcome types: knowledge, attitude, sensitivity, judgment, and behavior. Its core methodological claim is that "approaches that support the achievement of one type of learning outcome of RCR may not be as helpful in achieving other learning outcomes", so effect sizes must be analyzed separately per outcome rather than pooled. The taxonomy draws on prior taxonomies of moral-domain learning outcomes and RCR learning objectives, and structures the entire moderator and meta-regression analysis.
requirements: Outcome measures must be classifiable into one of the five types, and effect sizes calculated separately per outcome type
constraints: Two originally planned categories (basic skills, bias awareness) were dropped for lack of instances; attitude, behavior, and sensitivity were pooled as orientational outcomes where heterogeneity was low
target_learners: university students and professionals below doctoral level
target_learning_goals: responsible conduct of research
ethical decision-making
research integrity knowledge and attitudes
examples: The meta-analysis calculated separate effect sizes for knowledge, judgment, and pooled orientation outcomes, finding large deviations between these outcome groups
key_sources: Johannes Katsarov, Roberto Andorno, André Krom, Mariëtte van den Hoven. (2021). Effective Strategies for Research Integrity Training—a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:935–955. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09630-9

article_title: Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
citation: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9
title: Corpus of 28 randomized controlled trials of Chinese reading interventions
description: The evidence base of the meta-analysis: 28 independent RCT studies yielding 49 standardized mean-change effect sizes (37 for word reading and 12 for word spelling), identified through database searches of ERIC, PsycINFO, PubMed, ProQuest, and CNKI following PRISMA guidelines. Studies used pretest–posttest control-group designs with children with dyslexia or typically developing children, native Chinese speakers from preschool to sixth grade. Study characteristics coded included participant type, intervention method, outcome, implementer, duration, technology use, and form.
requirements: Included studies must provide sufficient statistics (sample sizes, means, and standard deviations) for computing effect size
constraints: Only randomized controlled trials were included; participants limited to school-aged native Chinese speakers with no other developmental, mental, or physical disorders
target_learning_goals: character/word reading
word spelling
examples: The initial database search resulted in 18814 records; 98 full-text articles were evaluated and 28 studies were finally included
key_sources: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9

article_title: Author Correction: The association between parental internalizing disorders and child school performance
citation: Magnus Nordmo, Thomas Kleppestø, Hans Fredrik Sunde, Martin Flatø, Perline Demange and Fartein Ask Torvik. (2023). Author Correction: The association between parental internalizing disorders and child school performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00195-6
title: Acknowledgements statement crediting Research Council of Norway funding (added by correction)

It states the work was supported by the Research Council of Norway, quoting: "This work was supported by the Research Council of Norway (grants number 300668)" and partly supported through its Centers of Excellence funding scheme (grant number 262700). It documents the funding provenance of the parental internalizing disorders and school performance study.

constraints: The correction changes only the Acknowledgements section; no substantive content of the original article is altered

article_title: Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. NCEE 2017-4026
citation: Kautz, T., Schochet, P., & Tilley, C. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation (NCEE 2017–4026). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.rct-yes.com
title: RCT-YES software package for design-based impact estimation
description: RCT-YES is a free software package funded by the Institute of Education Sciences that implements design-based methods for estimating impacts in randomized controlled trials. The report describes it as "a free, IES-funded software package that applies design-based methods to a range of experimental and non-experimental designs," and the study uses it to conduct all design-based re-analyses of the nine education RCTs. Its default settings encode a particular set of assumptions, including equal weighting of clusters and the finite-population framework.
requirements: Analysts must specify or accept the package's default assumptions about weighting, blocking, and the finite- versus super-population framework
constraints: By default RCT-YES weights blocks by the number of randomized units in the block and adopts the super-population framework only for matched pair designs
target_learners: education researchers with some training in statistical methods
target_learning_goals: conducting design-based impact analyses of experimental and non-experimental designs
examples: The report's design-based analyses across all nine RCTs were conducted using RCT-YES default and matched-assumption settings

article_title: The Evaluation of Effectiveness of Reciprocal Teaching Strategies on Comprehension of Expository Texts
citation: Gulhiz Pilten. (2016). The Evaluation of Effectiveness of Reciprocal Teaching Strategies on Comprehension of Expository Texts. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i10.1791
title: Reading Comprehension Evaluation Scale (RCES)
description: The RCES is a researcher-developed pre-post instrument with two parallel forms (A and B), each containing two expository texts from a Ministry-approved primary Turkish course book with intratextual, nontextual and intertextual questions, scored 0-4 per item with total scores ranging between 0 and 80. Reliability was supported by inter-rater Kendall W values, intra-rater Pearson correlations of 0.93 and 0.89, a test-retest correlation of 0.87, parallel-form correlation of 0.79 and Cronbach alpha of 0.90; content validity used the Lawshe technique with all item CVRs over 0.62.
requirements: Administered with 40 minutes per form; scoring follows the open-ended questions scoring key developed by NJDE (2014)
constraints: Developed for fourth-grade expository text comprehension in the Turkish primary context
target_learning_goals: expository text comprehension, including intratextual, nontextual and intertextual understanding
examples: Used as pre-test and post-test on all 54 work-group students in the study

title: Reading Comprehension Test (RCT) constructed on Barrett's Taxonomy
description: The RCT is the study's dependent measure, constructed by the researchers based on Barrett's Taxonomy. It contained 30 items in total: 16 literal level questions, 6 inferential level questions, 3 evaluative questions and 4 affective level questions. The instrument underwent a validity process and its reliability was tested with the KR20 Method, yielding a value of 0.65, which the authors deem "suitable and acceptable" citing Majid (2005).
requirements: Administered as pre and post test for both groups
constraints: Reliability of 0.65 is at the lower end of acceptability as the article itself frames it
target_learning_goals: Measuring reading comprehension across literal, inferential, evaluative and appreciation levels

article_title: Rapid cycle deliberate practice: a complement to clinical exposure in critical care education.
citation: Manetti Previero Bruno, Spataru Ana, Pinto Ruxandra, Piquette Dominique. (2026). Rapid cycle deliberate practice: a complement to clinical exposure in critical care education. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.1093/atsscholar/aapaf003
title: Rapid cycle deliberate practice (RCDP): short practice–feedback–rewind cycles with immediate correction of performance gaps
description: RCDP is a simulation technique aligned with the principles of deliberate practice but characterized by shorter cycles of practice—feedback—"scenario rewind"—practice again. Unlike traditional manikin-based simulation, it immediately addresses performance gaps instead of waiting until the end of the scenario, interrupting scenarios with multiple pauses for brief, task-oriented feedback and repeated practice of the same scenario section until performance is adequate. In this article it was implemented as fellow-facilitated, low-fidelity small-group sessions during ICU rotations.
requirements: Facilitators trained in the debriefing approach (here, a 60-minute interactive workshop plus paired supervision for first sessions) and a standardized debriefing script
constraints: The authors state the evidence base is inconsistent: not all studies comparing traditional and RCDP-based simulations demonstrated greater skill development, higher satisfaction, or confidence gains, and a meta-analysis highlighted inconsistencies in learning outcomes
target_learning_goals: key clinical tasks for initial care of acutely deteriorating inpatients, including airway management, hemodynamic instability, and hypoxia management
examples: Three 60-minute small-group RCDP training sessions with scenarios divided into three sections, mini-debriefings at section transitions, and safety-focused quick debriefings for critical errors
key_sources: Manetti Previero Bruno, Spataru Ana, Pinto Ruxandra, Piquette Dominique. (2026). Rapid cycle deliberate practice: a complement to clinical exposure in critical care education. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.1093/atsscholar/aapaf003

article_title: Rapid cycle deliberate practice: a complement to clinical exposure in critical care education.
citation: Manetti Previero Bruno, Spataru Ana, Pinto Ruxandra, Piquette Dominique. (2026). Rapid cycle deliberate practice: a complement to clinical exposure in critical care education. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.1093/atsscholar/aapaf003
title: Pragmatic weekly low-fidelity RCDP curriculum with rotating scenarios covering shared objectives and a formative capstone assessment
description: A four-week repeating simulation curriculum: three 60-minute small-group RCDP training sessions followed by a 30-minute individual formative traditional simulation-based assessment. Four realistic scenarios (hemorrhagic shock, status epilepticus, opioid intoxication, mixed respiratory failure) each embedded the same three clinical problems in variable contexts and order, so learners attending only one or two sessions were still exposed to all key tasks. Delivery used a basic portable manikin, pre-recorded sounds, an app-based monitor, and existing training material to minimize costs.
requirements: Scenarios designed from reviewed learning objectives, entrustable professional activities, and local rapid-response consultation data
Fellow facilitators trained via a 60-minute interactive workshop and paired with the core fellow for their first session
A 22-task checklist aligned with learning objectives for the formative assessment
constraints: The authors state it was impossible to determine how much of assessment performance was attributable to RCDP sessions, clinical exposure, concurrent teaching, or prior competencies; no pre-test was performed and RCDP was not compared with traditional simulation
target_learners: specialty residents from medicine, surgery, and anesthesia programs
target_learning_goals: management of circulatory shock, hypoxemic respiratory failure, and altered level of consciousness
examples: Weekly sessions scheduled on the same weekday afternoon during regular clinical daytime activities; assessment scores kept confidential from faculty and program directors
key_sources: Manetti Previero Bruno, Spataru Ana, Pinto Ruxandra, Piquette Dominique. (2026). Rapid cycle deliberate practice: a complement to clinical exposure in critical care education. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.1093/atsscholar/aapaf003

article_title: Rapid-cycle deliberate practice with an ex vivo porcine model of intussusception improves radiology residents' competence in air enema reduction.
citation: Xie Lichun, Mo Yongkang, Ma Jiejia, Xiao Yubin, Wu Xiaojia, Ma Xilun, Sun Danmiao, Ke Dongping, Mei Wei, Huang Ruibin. (2025). Rapid-cycle deliberate practice with an ex vivo porcine model of intussusception improves radiology residents' competence in air enema reduction. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08339-5
title: RCDP five-step chunked procedural training with iterative feedback until mastery
description: The training pattern breaks a complex clinical procedure into five sequenced steps (A: admission and consent; B: fluoroscopy and anal tube insertion; C: machine connection, pressure adjustment, diagnosis; D: postoperative fluoroscopy and instructions; E: machine cleaning and reassembly). After each step the trainee "paused for instructor feedback highlighting correct techniques and providing actionable improvements" and repeated the step until proficient before progressing. The authors state this chunking "effectively reducing the cognitive load of each module" for inexperienced residents.
requirements: An instructor who gives targeted feedback at the end of each step and judges proficiency before progression
Hands-on practice time per participant (30 minutes per resident in this study)
constraints: Temporal limitations in this study precluded incorporation of formal debriefing protocols, which the authors note may compromise educational outcomes
target_learners: radiology residents with no prior experience of the procedure
target_learning_goals: competence in air enema reduction of intussusception
examples: Residents in subgroups of four took turns as primary operator, completing step A, receiving feedback, and repeating until proficiency before advancing to step B
key_sources: Xie Lichun, Mo Yongkang, Ma Jiejia, Xiao Yubin, Wu Xiaojia, Ma Xilun, Sun Danmiao, Ke Dongping, Mei Wei, Huang Ruibin. (2025). Rapid-cycle deliberate practice with an ex vivo porcine model of intussusception improves radiology residents' competence in air enema reduction. article_title: Clinical simulation and deliberate practice in rapid-cycle deliberate practice: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: da Silva Gisele Cabral, Campanharo Cássia Regina Vancini, Lopes Maria Carolina Barbosa Teixeira, Okuno Meiry Fernanda Pinto, Miura Carla Roberta Monteiro, Batista Ruth Ester Assayag. (2025). Clinical simulation and deliberate practice in rapid-cycle deliberate practice: a randomized clinical trial. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2024-0632
title: Rapid-cycle deliberate practice: cycle-based simulation with feedback at the end of each cycle
description: Rapid-cycle deliberate practice (RCDP) is a simulation methodology, described as emerging in 2014, in which "the simulated clinical case" is "divided into cycles, which students repeat until the necessary competence is acquired". Feedback is delivered at the end of each cycle with quick pauses to correct errors and reinforce learning based on student performance, unlike standard clinical simulation where debriefing occurs after the scenario. In this trial the RCDP scenario was divided into four cycles and took 60 to 70 minutes, with corrective actions during cycles influencing whether students completed all cycles.
requirements: A validated clinical scenario divided into cycles with objectives expected for each phase
A facilitator who provides corrective feedback during cycles based on student performance
constraints: In this study RCDP took an average of 60 to 70 minutes per group, longer than the ten-minute SWSP scenario plus debriefing
In this trial RCDP was delivered individually, which students rated lower on collaboration than paired SWSP care
target_learning_goals: initial care for patients with suspected stroke, including assessment, scales, monitoring, and referral for imaging
examples: In the trial, the RCDP scenario was divided into four cycles addressing the expected objectives for each phase, with corrective actions and suggestions made during the cycles
key_sources: da Silva Gisele Cabral, Campanharo Cássia Regina Vancini, Lopes Maria Carolina Barbosa Teixeira, Okuno Meiry Fernanda Pinto, Miura Carla Roberta Monteiro, Batista Ruth Ester Assayag. (2025). Clinical simulation and deliberate practice in rapid-cycle deliberate practice: a randomized clinical trial. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2024-0632

article_title: RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs.
citation: Ayhan Muhammed, Kayadibi İsmail, Aykanat Berkehan. (2025). RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07483-2
title: RCFL dataset: 735 expert-labeled periapical radiographs of student root canal fillings
description: The RCFL dataset is a collection of periapical radiographs of root canal fillings performed by third-year dental students on extracted human teeth between 2023 and 2025, labeled by two expert clinicians as Acceptable or Unacceptable using the MakeSense program. As the article states, "a total of 735 PRs with dimensions of 418 × 836 pixels were collected to form a dataset named RCFL". Labels total 1069 acceptable and 902 unacceptable across 1971 root canal treatment procedures, split 655 for training and 80 for testing. The authors describe it as one of the first unique datasets for evaluating preclinical RCF procedures.
requirements: Images labeled by expert clinicians according to the acceptability of the RCF procedure relative to root canal filling length
constraints: Due to ethical considerations the dataset is not publicly available and is available from the corresponding author on reasonable request
Collected from a single institution using a single imaging device, which the authors say may limit generalizability
target_learners: third-year dental students in preclinical endodontics training
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of root canal filling length adequacy in preclinical endodontic procedures
examples: 655 images reserved for training and 80 for testing with the same splitting ratio applied throughout
key_sources: Ayhan Muhammed, Kayadibi İsmail, Aykanat Berkehan. (2025). RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07483-2

article_title: RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs.
citation: Ayhan Muhammed, Kayadibi İsmail, Aykanat Berkehan. (2025). RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07483-2
title: RCFLA-YOLO seven-stage framework for automated acceptability evaluation of root canal filling length
description: RCFLA-YOLO is a deep-learning framework that evaluates whether root canal filling length is acceptable in periapical radiographs, built on the YOLOv11 object detection architecture. The article describes that "the proposed method has been developed in seven stages", moving from data collection and expert labeling through preprocessing to 1280 × 640 pixels, training and testing of YOLOv11 variants, and confusion-matrix-based performance evaluation. The highest-performing variant (YOLOv11m) is incorporated into the proposed method, with output classes Length-Acceptable and Length-UnAcceptable.
requirements: Periapical radiographs labeled by expert clinicians as Acceptable or Unacceptable based on RCT suitability
Resizing of images to 1280 × 640 pixels before training
constraints: Focused solely on evaluating the adequacy of RCF length in single-rooted teeth, excluding complex canal configurations, resorption and severely curved roots
target_learners: third-year dental students in preclinical endodontics training
target_learning_goals: objective and automatic evaluation of root canal filling length acceptability in preclinical procedures
examples: Average processing measured at approximately 0.3 ms for preprocessing, 11.1 ms for inference and 0.7 ms for postprocessing, a total average of 12.1 ms per image
key_sources: Ayhan Muhammed, Kayadibi İsmail, Aykanat Berkehan. (2025). RCFLA-YOLO: a deep learning-driven framework for the automated assessment of root canal filling quality in periapical radiographs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07483-2

article_title: Rapid cycle deliberate practice simulation with standardized prebriefing and video based formative feedback in advanced cardiac life support.
citation: Kang Kyungja; Yu Mi. (2025). Rapid cycle deliberate practice simulation with standardized prebriefing and video based formative feedback in advanced cardiac life support. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97222-w
title: RCDP ACLS simulation program structure: standardized three-stage prebriefing, first simulation, video-based formative feedback with rerun, and structured debriefing
description: The article's program combines Ludlow's preparation, orientation, and pre-briefing stages with an RCDP cycle: a first simulation, viewing of a best-practice video with instructor formative feedback, a rerun of the same scenario, and a gather-analysis-summarize debriefing. The authors state that "RCDP frequently involves restarting simulations, each time increasing their complexity" and that feedback is "integrated during the exercises for on-the-spot learning and corrections". The program ran over three weeks with teams of 3–4 members.
requirements: Teams of 3–4 members with a high-fidelity simulator (SimMan 3G) and an instructor experienced in simulation education
constraints: Applying RCDP to complex scenarios can be challenging and may require more time and resources compared to traditional training methods due to its repetitive practice and immediate feedback structure
target_learning_goals: ACLS knowledge, self-efficacy, performance skills, and team communication in cardiac arrest resuscitation
examples: The experimental group completed prebriefing (about 2 h across preparation, orientation, and prebriefing), a first ACLS simulation, a 40–50 min video-based feedback session, and a rerun of the same scenario, followed by GAS-model debriefing.
key_sources: Kang Kyungja; Yu Mi. (2025). Rapid cycle deliberate practice simulation with standardized prebriefing and video based formative feedback in advanced cardiac life support. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97222-w

article_title: Development of a training programme to improve health literacy and respectful compassionate care competencies among undergraduate student nurses: a quantitative study.
citation: Kidayi Paulo L., Dausen Eyeshope J., Ndile Menti, Sixsmith Jane, Mawona Zuhura M., Berntsen Karin, Manangwa Saturini E., Smit Joya M., Rogathi Jane, de Zeeuw Janine. (2025). Development of a training programme to improve health literacy and respectful compassionate care competencies among undergraduate student nurses: a quantitative study. BMC Medical Education 25, 348. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06894-5
title: Developing respectful and compassionate care competencies requires integration into the hospital setting and clinical learning environment development, not education alone
description: The article argues that gaps in transferring respectful and compassionate care theory into practice "cannot be addressed by education alone but requires environmental culture change", and that compassionate care must be integrated into organizational infrastructure. Following the null training result, the authors propose that active inclusion of these competencies in the hospital setting and development of the clinical learning environment can facilitate nurses' competency development, supported by university-hospital collaboration.
requirements: Collaboration between universities and clinical settings
Continuous professional development in soft skills including communication skills for staff
constraints: Grounded in a single null pre-post finding in Tanzanian referral hospitals; the authors state the mechanism requires further exploration
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students on clinical placement
Practicing nurses and health care workers
target_learning_goals: Respectful and compassionate care
Transfer of learning into clinical practice
examples: After the programme, the referral hospitals established employee induction training programmes for all staff on respectful and compassionate care and health literacy

article_title: Interdisciplinary training program for pediatric cardiorespiratory arrest using rapid cycle deliberate practice: A descriptive cross-sectional study.
citation: Pereira RI, da Silva EMK. (2024). Interdisciplinary training program for pediatric cardiorespiratory arrest using rapid cycle deliberate practice: A descriptive cross-sectional study. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2023.0271.16022024
title: Rapid-cycle deliberate practice: simulation with in-scenario directive feedback and repeated cycles of increasing complexity until mastery
description: RCDP is a simulation-based education model, created by Hunt and grounded in Ericsson's deliberate practice, in which "learners develop their actions repeatedly (deliberate practice) for a short period (rapid cycle) in the same clinical scenario until the desired skill is mastered". When one cycle's objectives are met, a new cycle begins with increased task complexity. It "modifies the debriefing from traditional post-simulation feedback to directive feedback within an event": on non-conformity the scenario pauses, the instructor gives brief corrective information, and the scenario restarts correctly. The study applied it to pediatric CRA team training.
requirements: A facilitator/instructor who pauses the scenario on non-conformity and provides brief, pertinent corrective feedback
A clinical scenario sequenced into cycles with defined goals and increasing complexity
constraints: The authors state RCDP is best employed in simulations that require following a clearly defined script under time pressure, as in resuscitation scenarios
target_learners: Multidisciplinary hospital professionals (nurses, physicians, physical therapists) caring for pediatric patients
target_learning_goals: High-quality pediatric CPR and adherence to the pediatric cardiorespiratory arrest care algorithm
examples: A pediatric CRA case in PEA rhythm with four objective goals, delivered in 1-hour sessions of six participants, with 50 minutes of instruction including an uninterrupted baseline scenario followed by RCDP cycles.
key_sources: Pereira RI, da Silva EMK. (2024). Interdisciplinary training program for pediatric cardiorespiratory arrest using rapid cycle deliberate practice: A descriptive cross-sectional study. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2023.0271.16022024

article_title: Interdisciplinary training program for pediatric cardiorespiratory arrest using rapid cycle deliberate practice: A descriptive cross-sectional study.

title: One-hour RCDP session structure: objectives review, uninterrupted baseline scenario, 30 minutes of cycled RCDP practice, and closing feedback with performance graphs
description: The article's session design divides 1 hour into 50 minutes of instructional time and 10 minutes of course feedback and evaluation. Instruction begins with "the first 10 min for presenting the objectives, program strategy, and a punctual review of the CRA care algorithm", then 10 minutes of uninterrupted team performance for baseline data, then 30 minutes of RCDP in which incorrect actions pause the scenario for directed feedback and restart. Closing feedback shows each group a graph of compression quality before and after training.
requirements: Two instructors per round: one operating the scenario, one recording and extracting performance data
A high-fidelity manikin and compression-recording software to capture pre- and post-intervention data
constraints: Session size of six participants was determined by the institution's CRA care protocol
target_learning_goals: Mastery of the pediatric resuscitation algorithm and high-quality chest compressions
examples: Sessions ran November 2020 to May 2022; compression data from two professionals taking turns were recorded in the first and last cycles.

article_title: Rapid cycle deliberate practice versus postsimulation debriefing in pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation training: a randomized controlled study.
citation: Coelho Laila Pinto et al. (2024). Rapid cycle deliberate practice versus postsimulation debriefing in pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation training: a randomized controlled study. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2024AO0825
title: Rapid cycle deliberate practice: a simulation model combining repetitive practice, targeted feedback, mastery learning, and progressive difficulty
description: RCDP is a simulation instructional model the article describes as combining "repetitive practice, targeted feedback, mastery learning, and progressive difficulty". Sessions consist of consecutive rounds of increasing difficulty; learners must master predefined learning objectives before progressing. When the facilitator identifies a performance gap, the scenario is paused, direct feedback is given, and the scenario is repeated, creating a feedback-replay loop until mastery is achieved. The article contrasts this with PSD, which emphasizes reflection and discussion after scenario completion.
requirements: A psychologically safe environment where participants can welcome expert feedback
Predefined learning objectives and hard and soft stops to standardize sessions across groups
target_learning_goals: pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills and adherence to resuscitation algorithms
examples: In this study, RCDP sessions consisted of three consecutive 45-minute scenarios of increasing difficulty (respiratory arrest, nonshockable CPA, shockable CPA) with pausing and targeted feedback until mastery

title: Rapid cycle deliberate practice (RCDP) simulation protocol
description: RCDP is a simulation-based instructional strategy in which learners begin a simulated scenario that is "frequently paused by the instructor", with each break used for corrective instruction, coaching, feedback, and supervised repetition until skill mastery. In this study, facilitators used an RCDP coaching guide targeting time-sensitive ACLS interventions, paused, rewound, or resumed cases at their discretion, allowed role rotation, and fit simulation and debriefing into 45 minutes per case.
requirements: Facilitators trained in RCDP implementation by certified healthcare simulation instructors
A coaching guide focused on the target time-sensitive interventions
constraints: Frequent interruptions are inherent to the method, unlike uninterrupted immersive simulation
target_learners: Postgraduate year-1 internal medicine and emergency medicine residents
target_learning_goals: ACLS-based cardiopulmonary resuscitation team performance
examples: In this trial RCDP teams rotated roles and received real-time coaching against the same ACLS time-sensitive targets as the IS debriefing guide

Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11000545/
title: Use RCDP for algorithmic, procedurally demanding skills such as ACLS-based resuscitation
description: The article recommends RCDP where training content is algorithmic and procedural: "Instruction based in RCDP has strong evidence to support its use in areas of medical education that are algorithmic in nature, and/or require a high degree of procedural skill." The American Heart Association's 2020 guidelines recommend incorporating deliberate practice into BLS and ACLS training. In this study RCDP was applied to ACLS-based CPR for PGY-1 residents and shortened pause duration while improving learner perceptions.
requirements: Facilitators formally trained in both RCDP and immersive simulation facilitation
A coaching guide aligned to the targeted critical actions
constraints: The study found no significant differences on most timed metrics and was underpowered; skill retention was not assessed and quality of actions such as chest compression fraction was not measured
target_learning_goals: Time-critical resuscitation procedural skills and team performance
examples: Residents randomized to RCDP completed a subsequent immersive simulation in which their pause duration was 6.20 versus 14.20 seconds for IS teams

article_title: Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice: Application to Adult Advanced Life Support.
citation: Blanchard E, Booker D, Peterson DT, Carter T. (2022). Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice: Application to Adult Advanced Life Support. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11269
title: RCDP session structure: prebrief, progressive mastery of microskills with pause-rewind cycles, and closing debrief
description: The curriculum's session structure moves learners through scenarios of increasing difficulty: a 15-minute prebrief and orientation, a case stem, then facilitator pauses for feedback on microskills starting with initial assessment skills. "Learners were required to perfect each skill and repeatedly perform it perfectly throughout the simulation before moving on to the next," with cases rewound to the beginning until mastery of initial skills was achieved before advancing to skills such as defibrillator operation. A short group debriefing followed each case, with one hour dedicated to each case and debriefing.
requirements: Stopping points determined by learner actions rather than predetermined
Facilitators with RCDP-specific training
Checklists of critical actions for each case
constraints: One hour of time was dedicated to each case and debriefing
target_learning_goals: mastery of ACLS microskills
teamwork and communication
examples: Facilitators paused learners to coach on checking responsiveness and pulse before allowing progression to defibrillator operation
key_sources: Blanchard E, Booker D, Peterson DT, Carter T. (2022). Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice: Application to Adult Advanced Life Support. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11269

article_title: Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice: Application to Adult Advanced Life Support.
citation: Blanchard E, Booker D, Peterson DT, Carter T. (2022). Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice: Application to Adult Advanced Life Support. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11269
title: Three-case adult ACLS RCDP simulation curriculum (MedEdPORTAL)
description: A published curriculum of three in-person simulation cases for adult ACLS training using RCDP, set in a postanesthesia care unit with high-fidelity mannequins. "Scenarios in this curriculum are designed to be delivered in person and include pulseless ventricular tachycardia, unstable supraventricular tachycardia, and unstable sinus bradycardia." Each case includes simulation case files, critical-action flow charts, lab images, and a debriefing form as peer-reviewed appendices. It was designed for junior anesthesiology residents but is intended to generalize to other inpatient settings and specialties caring for adult patients.
requirements: High-fidelity mannequins
A resuscitation cart, a defibrillator with pads, IV pumps, and other code equipment
Physician and nonphysician instructors trained in simulation and RCDP
An attending anesthesiologist as content expert
constraints: Has only been used at one institution with anesthesiology residents; sample size relatively small
target_learners: other staff trained in ACLS caring for adult patients
target_learning_goals: effective teamwork and communication
role designation
defibrillator operation in manual mode
team leadership
applying ACLS algorithms
examples: Eighty-four postgraduate year 2 anesthesiology residents completed the curriculum over eight course offerings
key_sources: Blanchard E, Booker D, Peterson DT, Carter T. (2022). Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice: Application to Adult Advanced Life Support. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11269
